locomotive: The Locomotive is printed in Jerry Thomas's 1862 bar guide, widely regarded as the first American book of mixed drinks, as two egg yolks whisked with an ounce of honey, a little essence of cloves and a glass of curaçao into a pint of hot Burgundy. Leo Engel's London guide of 1878 repeats the recipe almost word for word. Neither book names a creator or explains the name, and hot egg drinks of this kind have since all but vanished from bar menus.
golden-slipper: The Golden Slipper is a pousse-café, a layered drink of yellow Chartreuse and egg yolk under a fruit spirit, and Jacques Straub printed it in his Drinks of 1914 topped with eau de vie de Danzig. Robert Vermeire's London guide of 1922 called it a South American pousse-café well known in Buenos Aires. No creator is recorded, and neither book explains the name.
bishop: Bishop is an English mulled drink of the eighteenth century, port warmed with sugar and an orange roasted with cloves, and it is often said to have been a favourite of Samuel Johnson. It gave its name to the smoking bishop that a reformed Scrooge promises to share with Bob Cratchit at the end of A Christmas Carol. It sits in a loose family of mulled wines named for church ranks, though old books disagree about which wine belongs to which rank.
arrack-punch: Punch is first recorded in English in the early seventeenth century, in a letter from an East India Company merchant in India, and the habit came home with the company's sailors and officers. The name is usually traced to the Hindi panch, five, for its ingredients, though that etymology is disputed. Arrack, distilled in Java and South Asia from cane, rice or palm sap, was among the first spirits used, and rack punch, as Londoners called it, was a famous treat at Vauxhall Gardens in the eighteenth century.
cambridge-milk-punch: The Cambridge Milk Punch is a hot English milk punch of brandy and rum whisked into warm milk with sugar, lemon and egg, and it carries the name of the university town, though no book records who first made it there or when.
regents-punch: Regent's Punch is named for George, Prince of Wales, who governed as Prince Regent during his father's illness before taking the throne as George IV, and whose household was known for lavish entertaining. Recipes vary, but they share a base of tea, citrus and several spirits finished with champagne, and Jerry Thomas included a version in his pioneering American bar guide. No record survives of who first mixed it, or whether the Regent ever drank it.
stone-wall: The Stone Wall pairs rum with hard cider, two everyday drinks of colonial New England, though bar books have hung the name on other mixes, Jerry Thomas's brandy and soda and Jacques Straub's whiskey and soda among them, and no one is recorded as its creator.
green-beast: The Green Beast was created by the French bartender Charles Vexenat around 2010 as a drink for Pernod Absinthe. He kept the build simple, one part each of absinthe, lime juice and sugar syrup lengthened with several parts of cold water over sliced cucumber, so that it could be made in a single glass or scaled up for a punch bowl. The water and citrus soften the anise of the spirit without hiding it.
newark: The Newark was created in 2007 by Jim Meehan and John Deragon at PDT in Manhattan, part of a run of drinks that New York bartenders built on the Brooklyn cocktail and named after places, from the Red Hook to the Bensonhurst. Making it with apple brandy pointed the name across the Hudson to New Jersey, home of Laird and Company, which holds US distilling licence number one and dates its commercial distilling to 1780.
marconi-wireless: The Marconi Wireless honours Guglielmo Marconi, whose transatlantic signals at the start of the twentieth century made wireless telegraphy the wonder of the day, and Albert Stevens Crockett preserved it among the drinks of the old Waldorf-Astoria bar in New York. It is apple brandy and Italian vermouth with orange bitters, the same pairing Jacques Straub printed as the Marconi in his Drinks of 1914. Who first mixed it is not recorded.
rattlesnake: The Rattlesnake was printed in 1930 in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book, compiled at the American Bar of the Savoy Hotel in London, as a batch for six of rye whiskey, sweetened lemon juice, egg whites and a few dashes of absinthe. Craddock explained the name with a joke about snakebite rather than any history. Like much of the book it slipped from view for decades, until the classic cocktail revival brought it back.
tia-mia: Ivy Mix created the Tia Mia in New York around 2010, splitting the rum of a Mai Tai with mezcal and giving it a name that rearranges the letters of the original. The lime, orgeat and orange curaçao of the Mai Tai stay in place. Mix later co-founded Leyenda in Brooklyn, a bar devoted to the spirits of Latin America, and the drink became one of those that carried mezcal into the tiki repertoire.
chrysanthemum-royale: The Chrysanthemum Royale tops the Chrysanthemum, the dry vermouth, Bénédictine and absinthe cocktail that the Savoy Cocktail Book called popular in the American bar of the liner Europa, with champagne in the usual Royale manner, and nobody has recorded who first did so.
bitter-elder: The Bitter Elder is a modern low-strength highball of elderflower liqueur, Campari and grapefruit lengthened with soda in the aperitivo manner, and neither its creator nor the date it first appeared has been published.
chartreuse-daisy: The Chartreuse Daisy applies the nineteenth-century daisy, spirit sharpened with citrus, sweetened and splashed with soda, to Green Chartreuse, the herbal liqueur of the Carthusian monks of the French Alps, and no creator or date is recorded for this version.
bensonhurst-fizz: The Bensonhurst Fizz lengthens the Bensonhurst, Chad Solomon's variation on the Brooklyn cocktail from Milk and Honey in Manhattan, with soda over ice, and nobody has recorded who first served it long.
oaxaca-sour: The Oaxaca Sour is a modern mezcal sour named for the southern Mexican state that makes most of the country's mezcal, its chilli-salt dusting borrowed from the sal de gusano served there with mezcal, and its creator and date have not been recorded.
harvard: The Harvard appears in George Kappeler's Modern American Drinks of 1895 as brandy and Italian vermouth with Angostura and a dash of gum syrup, stirred and topped with seltzer. The name points, by all appearances, to the university in Cambridge, Massachusetts, though no book records who first made it or why. It belongs to the family of vermouth cocktails that grew up beside the Manhattan in those decades.
duplex: The Duplex is printed in Jacques Straub's Drinks of 1914 as the Duplex or Albern Cocktail, Italian and French vermouth in equal measure with orange bitters, shaken, and its name simply describes that doubling. Vermouth-only cocktails of this kind were common in American bars before Prohibition and largely disappeared afterwards, until the modern taste for low-strength aperitif drinks brought them back.
vermouth-cocktail: The later, revised edition of Jerry Thomas's bar guide prints the Vermouth Cocktail as a glass of vermouth shaken with two dashes of bitters and strained over a slice of lemon, with gum syrup for customers who liked it sweet, beside a fancy version with maraschino. William Schmidt's The Flowing Bowl added a dash of absinthe. The drink dates from the decades when Italian and French vermouths were arriving in American bars.
absinthe-frappe: The Absinthe Frappé is credited to Cayetano Ferrer, who ran the Bourbon Street bar that became famous as the Old Absinthe House from the 1870s. Shaking absinthe over crushed ice made it a New Orleans hot-weather drink, and it was celebrated in the song Absinthe Frappé from Victor Herbert's 1904 musical It Happened in Nordland. Absinthe was banned in the United States in 1912, and the drink survived on substitutes until the ban was lifted in 2007.
absinthe-suissesse: The absinthe suissesse, whose name is French for a Swiss woman, is a New Orleans speciality of absinthe shaken with orgeat, egg white and cream. Stanley Clisby Arthur recorded the city's absinthe drinks in 1937 in Famous New Orleans Drinks and How to Mix 'Em, and the suissesse became a standard of French Quarter brunch, where restaurants such as Brennan's still pour it in the morning. Who first made it is not recorded.
roffignac: The Roffignac honours Count Louis Philippe de Roffignac, the French-born mayor of New Orleans for eight years in the early nineteenth century, who is credited with the city's first street lighting and paving. Made with cognac and a red raspberry syrup lengthened with soda, it was preserved by Stanley Clisby Arthur in his 1937 book of famous New Orleans drinks. Who first mixed it, and when, is not recorded.
alabazam: The Alabazam was printed in 1878 by Leo Engel, who tended the American bar at the Criterion in London, among the specialities of his own in his book American and Other Drinks: half a wine glass of brandy shaken with orange curaçao, lemon juice, sugar and a full teaspoon of Angostura. Engel did not explain the name. William Schmidt's The Flowing Bowl printed a version in New York in 1892, decades before the Sidecar made a similar balance famous.
fanciulli: The Fanciulli is preserved in Albert Stevens Crockett's Old Waldorf Bar Days of 1931, among the drinks remembered from the bar of the original Waldorf-Astoria in New York, as a Manhattan seasoned with Fernet-Branca. It is usually taken to honour Francesco Fanciulli, the Italian-born composer who succeeded John Philip Sousa as leader of the US Marine Band in 1892, though no book records who made it or why.
star-cocktail: The Star is printed in George Kappeler's Modern American Drinks as apple brandy and vermouth with gum syrup and Peychaud's or Angostura bitters, and Jacques Straub's Drinks gives it as applejack and Italian vermouth with orange bitters and a twist of lemon. It is one of a cluster of vermouth drinks that New York produced alongside the Manhattan, and who first named it is not recorded.
bombay-cocktail: Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 prints two Bombay Cocktails, one built on a punch liqueur and the other this aromatic mix of brandy with both vermouths, curaçao and a dash of absinthe. Neither has a recorded creator, and the name has no documented connection with the city, which was not unusual in a period that named drinks after distant places as readily as after people.
metropole: The Metropole takes its name from the Hotel Metropole near Times Square in New York, and its recipe was printed in George Kappeler's Modern American Drinks in 1895: brandy and French vermouth with gum syrup, Peychaud's and orange bitters and a maraschino cherry. The hotel later gained notoriety when the gambler Herman Rosenthal was shot outside it in 1912. Who first mixed the drink is not recorded.
metropolitan: George Kappeler's Modern American Drinks, published in New York, prints the Metropolitan beside the Metropole, as brandy and French vermouth with gum syrup and Angostura, and Jacques Straub's later Drinks adds a southern-style version with Italian vermouth and orange bitters, closer to this sweeter one. It has no connection with the much later vodka and cranberry Metropolitan, which simply borrowed the name.
third-rail: The Third Rail takes its name from the electrified rail that powers subway and elevated trains, a new hazard of city life in the early twentieth century. Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 prints two versions, one of them rum, apple brandy and brandy with a dash of absinthe. Its creator and first appearance have not been documented, and the recipe varies from book to book.
honeymoon: The Honeymoon is printed in Hugo Ensslin's Recipes for Mixed Drinks, published in New York in 1916, as apple brandy and Bénédictine with lemon juice and a few dashes of curaçao. It later turned up in other American bar books, but who created it, and where it was first mixed, are not recorded.
bosom-caresser: The Bosom Caresser is one of the specialities Leo Engel listed as his own in American and Other Drinks, written at the Criterion in London in 1878, where it was a whole egg shaken with strawberry syrup and a glass of brandy. Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 reworked it as brandy, curaçao and grenadine around an egg yolk, and noted that the golfers Bobby Jones and Francis Ouimet had both declared a preference for it.
deauville: The Deauville is printed in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book as equal parts brandy, calvados, Cointreau and lemon juice, a sidecar split between grape and apple brandy. It is named for the Normandy seaside resort that was a fashionable summer retreat for Parisians between the wars, in the same region as the orchards that make calvados. Who first mixed it, and when, is not recorded.
depth-bomb: The Depth Bomb takes a First World War name, after the depth charges dropped against submarines that were new weapons of that war, when bars named drinks after ordnance, most famously the French 75. Robert Vermeire's London guide of 1922 prints it as brandy and apple brandy with grenadine and lemon juice, and the Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 kept it. Its creator is not recorded.
chicago-cocktail: The Chicago is named for the city, and Robert Vermeire's London guide of 1922 describes it as a plain brandy cocktail with a little champagne on top, served in a glass rimmed with sugar, adding that it was also called the Fancy Brandy Cocktail. Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book printed it again in 1930. Who first made it, in Chicago or anywhere else, is not recorded.
brandy-champarelle: Jerry Thomas's 1862 bar guide prints the Brandy Champerelle among its fancy drinks as brandy, bitters and curaçao in a small wine glass, calling it a delicious French café drink. By the time George Kappeler's Modern American Drinks appeared in 1895 it had become a layered pousse-café of maraschino, curaçao, yellow Chartreuse and brandy, the style Thomas had also printed from Santina's saloon in New Orleans. The name has never been explained.
silver-fizz: William Schmidt's The Flowing Bowl, published in New York in 1892, already grades the gin fizz by egg, and the silver fizz is the base of the set, shaken with the white alone, which gives the drink the pale foam usually taken to explain its name. Fizzes were widely popular in America in the early twentieth century, especially in New Orleans, where Henry Ramos took the idea further with cream and orange flower water in his Ramos gin fizz.
golden-fizz: The golden fizz is the gin fizz made with an egg yolk instead of the white, and William Schmidt's The Flowing Bowl, published in New York in 1892, prints it as the silver fizz begun with the yolk. The yolk gives the drink its colour, the likely source of the name, and a fuller texture than the frothy silver fizz. No individual creator is recorded.
royal-fizz: The royal fizz completes the egg-graded family of gin fizzes: William Schmidt's The Flowing Bowl of 1892 makes it like the silver fizz but with the whole egg, and adds a grand royal fizz with orange juice, maraschino and a dash of parfait amour. Fizzes were among the most popular drinks in American bars around the turn of the twentieth century, and no individual creator is recorded for this one.
diamond-fizz: Jacques Straub's Drinks of 1914 prints the Diamond Fizz as a gin fizz filled up with champagne instead of soda water, which makes it a close relation, sometimes an identical one, of the French 75, and the two names have often been used for the same drink. No creator is recorded.
gin-daisy: The daisy first appears in a bar book in the 1876 edition of Jerry Thomas's guide, in gin, brandy, whiskey and rum versions, as a sour sweetened with a cordial and given a splash of soda. Later recipes moved toward grenadine and crushed ice. The origin of the name is unknown. The Margarita is often read as a tequila daisy, since margarita is Spanish for daisy, though that is only one of several competing accounts of its origin.
brandy-daisy: The brandy daisy was among the daisies Jerry Thomas added to the 1876 edition of his bar guide, when brandy was still a common base for American mixed drinks, and his 1887 revision makes it with curaçao, gum syrup, lemon juice and a dash of Jamaica rum, topped with seltzer. Who first called the drink a daisy, and why, has never been established, and the name has since been applied to quite different recipes.
whiskey-daisy: The whiskey daisy is one of the daisies Jerry Thomas printed in the 1876 edition of his bar guide, alongside gin, brandy and rum versions. His 1887 revision makes it with bourbon or rye, lemon juice, gum syrup and orgeat, shaken and topped with seltzer, while grenadine and crushed ice arrived with later books. Its name, like the rest of the family's, has no recorded explanation.
gin-fix: The fix appears in Jerry Thomas's 1862 bar guide, widely regarded as the first American book of mixed drinks, in brandy, gin and Santa Cruz rum versions: spirit, sugar, a little water and lemon stirred over shaved ice and dressed with fruit in season. Thomas made his sour from the same ingredients, leaving out all the fruit but a piece of lemon. Who first called the drink a fix is not recorded.
whiskey-fix: The Whiskey Fix puts bourbon into the fix, spirit, lemon and sugar over shaved ice under a heap of fruit, a form Jerry Thomas printed in brandy, gin and rum versions, and no one is credited with first making it with whiskey.
whiskey-cobbler: Jerry Thomas printed a whiskey cobbler among the cobblers in his 1862 bar guide. The form had become a sensation in American bars over the previous decades in its sherry version, wine with sugar and fruit over a heap of shaved ice, and it helped make the drinking straw a bar fixture. The origin of the name is uncertain; one common explanation points to the cobblestone-like pieces of ice.
brandy-cobbler: The Brandy Cobbler applies the cobbler, the shaved-ice, sugar and fruit drink whose sherry version became an American sensation and earned a scene in Dickens's Martin Chuzzlewit, to the brandy that was then the common spirit of the American bar, and no one is credited with it.
whiskey-rickey: The rickey was born in the 1880s at Shoomaker's bar in Washington, where the bartender George Williamson squeezed lime into the bourbon and sparkling water ordered by Colonel Joe Rickey, a Democratic lobbyist. The drink took Rickey's name, which by his own account frustrated him, since he hoped to be remembered for more. Gin rickeys overtook the original by the 1890s, but the whiskey version came first.
pierre-collins: The Pierre Collins is the cognac member of the Collins family, the tall lemon, sugar and soda drinks that entered American print as the Tom Collins, and its French name follows the bar habit of giving each spirit its own Collins rather than recording any inventor.
pedro-collins: The Pedro Collins is the rum member of the Collins family, descended from the John Collins associated with a headwaiter at Limmer's Hotel in London and the Tom Collins of American bar books, and no creator or date is recorded for it.
bamboo-royale: The Bamboo Royale tops the Bamboo, the dry sherry and vermouth cocktail usually credited to Louis Eppinger at the Grand Hotel in Yokohama, with champagne in the familiar Royale manner, and no one has recorded who first did so.
port-sangaree: The sangaree was drunk in Britain and its Caribbean colonies by the eighteenth century, a wine or spirit diluted with water, sweetened and dusted with nutmeg, and its name shares a root with the Spanish sangría, from sangre, blood. Port, shipped to Britain in quantity under its long trade alliance with Portugal, made one of the classic versions, and Jerry Thomas still printed a port wine sangaree in his American bar guide. No single creator is recorded.
sherry-sangaree: The sangaree, an eighteenth-century British and Caribbean mix of wine or spirit with water, sugar and nutmeg, takes its name from the same root as the Spanish sangría. Sherry was one of the most widely drunk wines in Britain and America through much of the nineteenth century, and Jerry Thomas printed a sherry sangaree among the versions in his pioneering bar guide. No creator is recorded for it.
brandy-sangaree: Jerry Thomas's pioneering bar guide, widely regarded as the first American book of mixed drinks, printed the sangaree in a run of versions, port, sherry, brandy, gin, ale and porter, treating it as a template rather than a single recipe. The form itself is older, a sweetened, nutmeg-dusted wine or spirit drink known in Britain and the Caribbean in the eighteenth century, and its name is related to the Spanish sangría. No individual is credited with the brandy version.
rum-flip: Flip was a staple of colonial New England taverns: beer, rum and molasses or sugar in a tankard, heated by plunging in a red-hot iron called a loggerhead, which made the mixture foam. The word is recorded in English from the end of the seventeenth century, and the drink stayed popular in American and English taverns into the nineteenth. Later bar books turned the flip into a cold drink shaken with a whole egg, and no individual is credited with any version.
sherry-flip: The Sherry Flip is the wine member of the flip family, which began as a hot tavern mix of beer, spirit and sugar and became a cold drink shaken with a whole egg, and no creator is recorded for the sherry version.
whiskey-flip: The Whiskey Flip is the American whiskey member of the flip family, spirit shaken with a whole egg and sugar and dusted with nutmeg, a cold descendant of the hot tavern flip that no one is credited with first making with whiskey.
ale-flip: Flip is recorded in English from the end of the seventeenth century, when it was known as a sailors' drink, and it began as ale or beer mixed with spirit and sugar and heated by plunging a red-hot loggerhead from the fire into the tankard, which made it foam. Jerry Thomas's pioneering bar guide still printed an ale flip of boiling ale beaten into eggs, sugar and nutmeg and poured from jug to jug until smooth and frothed.
whiskey-toddy: The toddy takes its name from the Hindi tari, the fermented palm sap that British traders met in India, and by the eighteenth century the word meant a spirit mixed with water and sugar. Jerry Thomas's pioneering bar guide prints the whiskey toddy as sugar, water and whiskey over a lump of ice, made hot with boiling water, and turns it into a sling simply by grating nutmeg on top. Unlike many later hot toddies it has no lemon.
brandy-toddy: Spirit with sugar and water is among the oldest American mixed drinks, and Jerry Thomas's pioneering bar guide prints the brandy toddy as sugar, water and brandy over ice, with boiling water in place of the ice for the hot version. The word toddy came into English from the Hindi tari, palm sap. Brandy was a common spirit in American bars until phylloxera devastated the French vineyards later in the nineteenth century, after which whiskey largely took its place.
rum-toddy: The Rum Toddy is the colonial New England toddy, rum distilled locally from Caribbean molasses stirred with sugar and hot water and finished with nutmeg, a household winter habit that no one is credited with inventing.
whiskey-sling: The sling is one of the oldest American mixed drinks, spirit with sugar and water and a grating of nutmeg, served hot or cold. When a newspaper in Hudson, New York, printed the first known definition of the cocktail early in the nineteenth century, it called the cocktail a bittered sling, which makes the sling the older form. Jerry Thomas's pioneering bar guide prints a hot whiskey sling of whiskey and boiling water under nutmeg, and no single creator is recorded.
brandy-sling: Slings, spirit sweetened and diluted with water and topped with nutmeg, were common in American taverns by the eighteenth century, and brandy slings were among the standard versions. Jerry Thomas's pioneering bar guide makes the brandy sling exactly as the brandy toddy, with nutmeg grated on top. The origin of the word is uncertain, and the name later passed to grander drinks such as the Singapore Sling.
gin-sour: The sour first appears in a bar book in Jerry Thomas's 1862 guide, widely regarded as the first American book of mixed drinks, in brandy, gin and Santa Cruz rum versions, made like the fix of spirit, sugar, water and lemon but without the fruit. The gin sour is one of those originals. The template went on to become the backbone of a whole branch of cocktails, from the daisy and the fizz to the Sidecar and the Margarita.
rum-sour: The rum sour is as old as the sour in print: Jerry Thomas's 1862 bar guide notes that a Santa Cruz sour is made with rum from St Croix, then a Danish island in the Caribbean, in place of the gin. Made with lemon rather than the lime of the later Cuban Daiquiri, it shows how the same structure took on different citrus in different places. No individual is credited with the rum sour.
applejack-sour: The Applejack Sour puts the apple brandy of New Jersey, long made by Laird and Company, holder of US distilling licence number one, on the old sour template of spirit, lemon and sugar, and no one is credited with it.
gin-crusta: The crusta appears in Jerry Thomas's 1862 bar guide in brandy, whiskey and gin versions, and Thomas wrote that it was said to have been invented by Santina, a celebrated Spanish caterer, usually identified today as Joseph Santini of the Jewel of the South in New Orleans. The name is usually explained by the crust of sugar on the rim of the glass, above a whole lemon peel lining the inside. The gin version has always been rarer than the brandy original.
whiskey-crusta: Jerry Thomas's 1862 bar guide printed the crusta in brandy, whiskey and gin versions, making the whiskey one exactly like the brandy with whiskey in its place, and credited the form to a New Orleans caterer called Santina, now usually identified as Joseph Santini. Its name refers to the crust of sugar on the glass's rim. The whiskey crusta never matched the fame of the brandy one, which bartenders often cite as an ancestor of the Sidecar.
brandy-julep: The julep is first described in America early in the nineteenth century, as a morning dram of spirit with mint taken by Virginians, and in its early days it was often made with cognac or peach brandy rather than whiskey. Its name comes, via Arabic and French, from the Persian gulab, rosewater. Jerry Thomas's pioneering bar guide made its mint julep with cognac and its brandy julep the same way without the fancy fruit, and bourbon became the standard only as American whiskey rose.
champagne-julep: The Champagne Julep is one of the grander variations of the julep, which nineteenth-century American bars made on almost any base, mint and sugar under sparkling wine and crushed ice, and no individual is credited with it.
remsen-cooler: The Remsen Cooler is printed in William Boothby's American Bar-Tender of 1891, which says it was introduced by William Remsen, a retired naval officer and popular member of the Union Club in New York, and Boothby made it with Old Tom gin, a long lemon peel and soda. By 1922 Robert Vermeire's London guide made it with Remsen's Scotch whisky instead, and Scotch became the usual base, so the drink carries two competing stories.
klondike-cooler: The Klondike Cooler takes its name from the Yukon gold rush at the end of the nineteenth century, a whiskey cooler of orange juice and ginger ale over a long orange peel, and who first made it is not recorded.
harvard-cooler: The Harvard Cooler is printed in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 as applejack or calvados shaken with lemon or lime juice and sugar and lengthened with soda water in a long tumbler. It shares its name with the Harvard, the brandy and vermouth cocktail named for the university, but not its recipe, and its creator is not recorded.
bombo: Bombo, or bumbo, was a plain mix of rum, water, sugar and nutmeg drunk by sailors, soldiers and colonists across the eighteenth-century Atlantic, from the Caribbean to the American colonies. It was common enough in Virginia that candidates treated voters to it, and George Washington's papers from his first successful campaign for the House of Burgesses record rum bought for that purpose. The origin of the name is uncertain, and no single creator is recorded.
blackstrap: Blackstrap is a cheap colonial New England mix of rum and molasses, both plentiful in a region whose distilleries turned Caribbean molasses into rum, and no creator or date is on record.
shandygaff: Shandygaff, beer or ale mixed with ginger beer, is recorded in English from 1853, and the origin of the word is obscure. The shorter word shandy, first recorded in 1888, began as an abbreviation of it, and the lemonade version that most people now order came later. H. G. Wells gave the drink a cameo in The History of Mr Polly, where a shandygaff is mixed from beer and ginger beer in a round-bellied jug.
green-swizzle: The Green Swizzle was a fixture of Caribbean bars in the early twentieth century, found in Trinidad, Barbados and Grenada, and a Trinidad cookery handbook of 1907 is among its earliest records. Its green came from wormwood bitters, with falernum as the sweetener, not from the crème de menthe of some later versions. P. G. Wodehouse gave it lasting fame in 1924, when Bertie Wooster sang its praises after a visit to the West Indian section of the British Empire Exhibition at Wembley.
zoom: The Zoom is a short interwar drink of spirit, honey and cream with the base left to the drinker, brandy, whisky or gin, and neither its creator nor the reason for its name is recorded.
scaffa: The scaffa is an old class of drink served without ice and at room temperature, spirit and liqueur built straight into the glass with bitters. Jerry Thomas's 1862 bar guide prints a brandy scaffa of brandy and maraschino with two dashes of bitters, and Leo Engel's London guide of 1878 gives the same, close to the layered pousse-cafés it resembles. The meaning of the name has never been explained.
cardinale: The Cardinale is usually credited to Giovanni Raimondo at the bar of the Hotel Excelsior in Rome in the 1950s, though it was once attributed to Harry's Bar in Venice. His version is said to have used Riesling with the gin and Campari, where later recipes, the IBA's among them, settled on dry vermouth. The name is generally put down to its cardinal-red colour, though some accounts link it to a visiting cardinal.
pirlo: The Pirlo is the traditional aperitivo of Brescia, still white wine with a red bitter and a splash of soda, a cousin of the Venetian spritz whose name is usually explained from the Brescian dialect after the way the bitter spirals down through the wine, and no creator or date is recorded.
hugo: The Hugo was invented in 2005 by Roland Gruber at the San Zeno bar in Naturns, in South Tyrol, as a light aperitif of prosecco with mint. His original used lemon balm syrup; elderflower syrup or liqueur replaced it as the drink spread through the Alps and into Germany and Austria. Gruber has said the name was a chance choice, and that he first thought of calling it Otto.
kaisermelange: The Kaisermelange, the emperor's mélange, is one of the many named coffees of the Viennese coffee house, black coffee whisked with an egg yolk and honey and laced with brandy, and no one has recorded who first made it.
kafi-luz: Kafi Luz is a farmhouse and tavern habit of central Switzerland around Lucerne, pale weak coffee poured over sugar with a fruit brandy such as Träsch or plum schnapps, and it has no recorded creator.
eierpunsch: Eierpunsch, egg punch, is a German winter drink of white wine beaten with egg yolks, sugar and vanilla over gentle heat and sold beside Glühwein at Christmas markets, a household and market tradition with no recorded creator.
maibowle: Maibowle, the May punch of Germany, is traced to a wine flavoured with sweet woodruff that the Benedictine monk Wandalbert of Prüm Abbey mentioned in 854. The herb is picked in spring before it flowers and wilted briefly so that its scent develops, then steeped in white wine that is topped with sparkling wine. It is still made in late April and May, especially for May Day, and across the border in Belgium the town of Arlon makes a version called Maitrank.
diesel: Diesel is the German pub name for lager mixed half and half with cola, one of several beer and soft-drink mixes that go by regional names such as Krefelder with Altbier and Colaweizen with wheat beer, and no one is credited with the mix or its name.
kaffekask: Kaffekask is a Swedish rural custom of coffee laced with brännvin in the same cup, especially associated with the north of the country and close kin to the Norwegian karsk, and it has no recorded creator or date.
svarak: Svařák is the everyday Czech name for svařené víno, mulled wine, sold from stalls at the Christmas markets of Prague and other towns as part of the central European family of spiced hot wines, and it has no recorded creator or date.
hriato: Hriatô, whose name means warmed, is a winter drink of the Slovak mountain regions of Liptov, Orava and Spiš, honey or caramelised sugar heated with bacon or butter and a local spirit, traditionally served around Christmas, with no recorded creator.
sumadijski-caj: Šumadijski čaj, Šumadija tea, is a winter drink from the plum country of central Serbia that contains no tea, rakija heated with sugar or honey and served hot in a tea glass, a folk tradition with no recorded creator.
arak-limonana: Limonana, from the Hebrew limon, lemon, and nana, mint, is a word coined in Israel in the 1990s for an advertising campaign promoting bus advertising, in which well-known faces endorsed a drink of that name that turned out to be fictional. The frozen lemon and mint drink that followed became a fixture of Israeli summers, and adding arak, the anise spirit of the Levant, turned it into a bar drink, though no one is credited with that combination.
poktanju: Poktanju means bomb liquor in Korean, a shot of soju or whisky dropped into a glass of beer, and it became a fixture of South Korean social life in the second half of the twentieth century. Accounts of how it started differ, crediting office workers of the boom years, officers back from training in America or a meeting of prosecutors, police and journalists in Chuncheon, and none is settled.
subak-soju: Subak soju, subak being Korean for watermelon, is a party serve of Korean pubs and summer gatherings in which a hollowed watermelon is filled with its own flesh blended with soju and shared at the table, and no creator or date is recorded.
arak-attack: Arak Attack is a tourist-bar pun on Bali's own spirit, the island's palm or rice arak mixed with orange juice under a red float, and neither the person who coined the name nor the date is recorded.
arrack-sour: The Arrack Sour applies the classic sour of spirit, lime and sugar to Sri Lankan arrack, distilled from the sap of unopened coconut flowers that tappers collect high in the palms, and no individual creator or date is recorded.
bandera: The Bandera, Spanish for flag, is a serving custom of Mexico's tequila country rather than one bar's recipe, three glasses of lime juice, blanco tequila and sangrita set side by side in the green, white and red of the flag and sipped in turn, with no recorded creator.
batida: Batida, from the Portuguese for beaten or shaken, is a Brazilian family of cachaça drinks blended or shaken with fruit or coconut and often sweetened with condensed milk, a popular tradition rather than the invention of any one bar, with no recorded creator.
ponche-a-la-romana: Ponche a la romana is a Chilean party drink of sparkling wine poured over pineapple ice cream for New Year and the national holidays, its name echoing the iced punch à la romaine of grand nineteenth-century dinners, and no creator or date is recorded.
papelon-con-limon-y-ron: Papelón con limón is an everyday Venezuelan drink of papelón, unrefined cane sugar sold in hard cones, dissolved in water and sharpened with lime, and adding rum turns the household refreshment into a long drink with no recorded creator.
rum-and-ting: Ting, a sparkling grapefruit soda, was first produced in Jamaica in 1976 by Desnoes and Geddes, so Rum and Ting can be no older than that. Paired with Jamaican white overproof rum, it became one of the island's everyday highballs, the kind of order that needs no recipe, and nobody is credited with first mixing the two.
ponche-de-creme: Ponche de crème is the Christmas eggnog of Trinidad and Tobago, eggs, milk, rum and spice seasoned with the Angostura bitters made in Port of Spain, a family recipe rather than an invention, with no recorded creator.
springbok: The Springbok shooter layers green crème de menthe under Amarula, the South African cream liqueur made from marula fruit, in the green and gold of the national rugby team named for the antelope, and no creator or date is recorded.
sour-de-maracuya: The Sour de Maracuyá reworks the Pisco Sour, usually credited to the American bartender Victor Morris at his bar in Lima, with passion fruit, one of many local-fruit versions served in Peru, and no individual is credited with this one.
attention: The Attention is a pale lilac drink of absinthe, gin, crème de violette and dry vermouth in equal parts, and neither its creator, its first printing nor the meaning of its name is recorded.
bennett: Robert Vermeire's London guide of 1922 prints the Bennett as Old Tom gin with fresh lime juice and two dashes of Angostura, and says it was very popular in Chile, where it was named after a well-known landowner of that country. Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 kept it with dry gin, and neither book gives Bennett's first name or the bartender who made it.
colony: The Colony is named for the Colony, the New York restaurant that became one of the city's most fashionable dining rooms under its proprietor Gene Cavallero and is said to have served its regulars discreetly during Prohibition. The drink, gin with grapefruit and maraschino, is usually dated to that period and sometimes credited to the bartender Marco Hattem, though the attribution is uncertain and no exact date is recorded.
commodore: Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 prints the Commodore as Canadian whisky with lime or lemon juice, a little syrup and orange bitters, while other books of the period use the name for quite different drinks. No single creator, bar or date is attached to it, and the name, a naval rank, was one of many military and naval titles borrowed by drinks of the time.
duchess: Jacques Straub's Drinks, published in Chicago in 1914, prints the Duchess as absinthe with French and Italian vermouth in equal thirds, shaken, and Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 carried it to London. It is one of a handful of classic drinks in which absinthe is the base rather than a seasoning, and its creator and the reason for the name are not recorded.
earthquake: The Earthquake is printed in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 as equal parts gin, whisky and absinthe, with a joking note on the name and a warning about its strength. It is often compared with the tremblement de terre of cognac and absinthe that legend attributes to the painter Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec. No creator is recorded for the London drink.
fourth-degree: Robert Vermeire's London guide of 1922 describes the Fourth Degree as a Martini in the Continental style with a dash of absinthe, gin with dry and sweet vermouth in equal measure, and Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 prints it the same way with four dashes of absinthe. The origin of the name is not recorded.
gin-and-it: Gin and It is British bar shorthand for gin and Italian, the sweet vermouth that Turin houses such as Martini and Cinzano exported in the nineteenth century, a plain pairing traditionally poured without ice and with no recorded creator or date.
grand-slam: The Grand Slam is printed in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 as Swedish punsch with French and Italian vermouth. Its name is the card players' term for taking every trick, from whist and bridge. Swedish punsch, built on the Batavia arrack that the Swedish East India Company began importing from Java in the eighteenth century, was a fashionable bottle in the bars of the period. Its creator is not recorded.
hoop-la: The Hoop La is printed in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 as equal parts lemon juice, Kina Lillet, Cointreau and brandy, and the same formula appears elsewhere in the book under other names, the Frank Sullivan and the Odd McIntyre, after two American newspaper writers of the day. It shares its four-equal-parts structure with the Corpse Reviver No. 2. Its creator is not recorded.
maidens-blush: Robert Vermeire's London guide of 1922 gives a Maiden's Blush of gin and grenadine with a dash of an absinthe-style spirit as a recipe of Frank Newman of Paris, and Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 prints two drinks under the name, one of gin with curaçao, grenadine and lemon, the other built with absinthe. The name was a period term for a pale pink, the colour the grenadine gives.
moonlight: The Moonlight is a dry short drink of kirsch, grapefruit juice and a little sugar, and its creator, first printed source and the reason for its name have not been recorded.
nineteen-twenty: Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 prints a Nineteen-Twenty of kirsch, gin and French vermouth with a teaspoon of groseille syrup and a dash of absinthe, named, by all appearances, for the year, and the same book has a Nineteen-Twenty Pick-Me-Up of absinthe and gin. The version with sweet vermouth has no recorded source, and no creator is named for any of them.
prince-of-wales: The Prince of Wales is credited to Albert Edward, Prince of Wales, the future Edward VII, by an anonymous biography of 1901 written by a member of the royal household, which says he composed a cocktail of rye whisky, pineapple, maraschino, bitters, lemon peel and a little champagne. He was heir to the throne for nearly sixty years and well known for his love of society and entertaining, and the attribution has stayed with the drink ever since.
soul-kiss: Jacques Straub's Drinks, published in Chicago in 1914, already prints several Soul Kiss cocktails, one of them rye with Dubonnet, French vermouth and a spoonful of orange juice, and Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 carries a close version with Canadian whisky. Neither book names a creator or explains the name. Dubonnet's own story credits Joseph Dubonnet with creating his quinine aperitif in Paris for French soldiers in North Africa.
southern-bride: The Southern Bride is a short gin drink of grapefruit juice with a touch of maraschino, close kin to the Colony, and its creator, first printed source and the meaning of its name have not been documented.
whist: The Whist is printed in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book as calvados with Bacardi rum and Italian vermouth, and Craddock's note calls it a drink known in the West Indies for countless years, a kind of West Indian sundowner. It shares its name with the card game, but neither its creator nor the reason for the name is recorded.
improved-holland-gin-cocktail: The later, revised edition of Jerry Thomas's bar guide prints an improved gin cocktail made like his improved brandy cocktail, with gum syrup, bitters, maraschino, absinthe and a twist of lemon, and Holland or Old Tom gin in place of the brandy. The improved cocktails dressed up the plain mix of spirit, sugar, water and bitters, and Holland gin, or genever, was then a common gin in American bars. Drinkers who preferred the plain version later began asking for their cocktails the old-fashioned way.
fancy-brandy-cocktail: The Fancy Brandy Cocktail is printed in Jerry Thomas's 1862 bar guide, widely regarded as the first American book of mixed drinks, as the plain brandy cocktail strained into a fancy wine glass with a piece of lemon peel on top and the rim moistened with lemon. Thomas used fancy for dressed-up versions of standard drinks, and the grades of plain, fancy and later improved show how carefully bartenders of the period told one variation from another.
absinthe-cocktail: The later, revised edition of Jerry Thomas's bar guide prints the Absinthe Cocktail as a pony of absinthe with two dashes of anisette and one of Angostura, lengthened with a stream of iced water, shaken and strained, the slow drip turned into a cocktail. New Orleans, with its French heritage, was the American city most closely tied to absinthe, though no individual creator is recorded.
rum-old-fashioned: The Rum Old Fashioned applies the original cocktail of spirit, sugar, water and bitters, which drinkers began ordering the old-fashioned way as bartenders added liqueurs, to aged rum, a common choice in the modern revival, and no one is credited with it.
morning-glory: The later, revised edition of Jerry Thomas's bar guide prints a Morning Glory Cocktail of brandy and whiskey together, stirred with gum syrup, curaçao, bitters and a dash of absinthe and topped with seltzer, one of several morning drinks of the period. Later books used the name for a fizz as well. Its creator and the place where it was first mixed are not recorded.
artillery: The Artillery is printed in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 as dry gin and Italian vermouth, one of the many gin and vermouth combinations of the period. No creator or date is recorded, and the military name follows the period habit of naming drinks after weapons and regiments.
diki-diki: Robert Vermeire wrote that he introduced the Diki-Diki at the Embassy Club in London in February 1922, and he printed it that year in Cocktails: How to Mix Them as calvados with Swedish punsch and grapefruit juice. He named it after Diki-Diki, whom his book describes as the ruler of an island in the southern Philippines. Harry Craddock carried it into the Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930.
deshler: The Deshler appears in Hugo Ensslin's Recipes for Mixed Drinks, published in New York in 1916, as rye and Dubonnet with Peychaud's bitters, a little Cointreau and twists of orange and lemon. Accounts of its name differ: some tie it to the featherweight boxer Dave Deshler, others to the Deshler Hotel in Columbus, Ohio, and none is settled.
frisco: The Frisco is a short rye drink of Bénédictine and lemon that carries San Francisco's nickname, and no bartender or bar there has a documented claim to it.
barbary-coast: The Barbary Coast is named for the old saloon and red-light district of San Francisco, which drew sailors and gold seekers from the second half of the nineteenth century until reformers closed it down early in the twentieth. The drink, gin and Scotch with crème de cacao and cream, is printed in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, but its creator and first appearance are not recorded.
suissesse: The suissesse, French for a Swiss woman, is an absinthe drink shaken with egg white and anisette that New Orleans adopted as its own. Stanley Clisby Arthur's Famous New Orleans Drinks and How to Mix 'Em recorded the city's absinthe drinks in 1937, and the suissesse has remained a fixture of French Quarter brunch. Who first made it is not recorded.
cafe-brulot: Café brûlot is a New Orleans tableside coffee of brandy, spices and citrus peel set alight and ladled, and Antoine's, the French Quarter restaurant, credits its creation to Jules Alciatore, son of the founder, in the 1890s. The name comes from the French brûler, to burn, and the full name on some menus is café brûlot diabolique. It became a showpiece of the city's old Creole restaurants, served from special bowls with long ladles.
la-louisiane: La Louisiane was the house cocktail of the Restaurant de la Louisiane, one of the old Creole restaurants of the French Quarter, and Stanley Clisby Arthur recorded it in 1937 in Famous New Orleans Drinks and How to Mix 'Em, describing it as out of the ordinary as the dishes on the restaurant's menu. Rye, sweet vermouth, Bénédictine and absinthe place it in the same family as the Vieux Carré and the Sazerac.
gun-shop-fizz: The Gun Shop Fizz was created by Kirk Estopinal at Cure, the New Orleans cocktail bar on Freret Street, and it turns the usual logic of a drink upside down by using Peychaud's bitters as the base rather than as a seasoning, with citrus, fruit and soda. It shows how far modern bartenders pushed the old New Orleans bitters, though the drink's date and the story behind its name have not been widely published.
milk-punch: The earliest known recipe for milk punch appears in an English cookbook of 1711, and the drink became an eighteenth-century favourite, prized because it could be bottled and kept. Its secret is curdling: milk is added to spirit, citrus and spice so that it splits, and straining off the curds leaves a clear, stable punch. Benjamin Franklin recorded his own version in 1763, and the technique returned to bars in the modern cocktail revival.
brandy-milk-punch: Brandy milk punch is the New Orleans brunch version of the old milk punches of Britain and America, brandy, milk, sugar and vanilla shaken cold and dusted with nutmeg rather than clarified, and no creator or date is recorded.
claret-cup: Claret cup is one of the long wine cups of Victorian England, red Bordeaux lengthened with soda and citrus and scented with cucumber and borage for garden parties and summer picnics, and recipes fill the period's books without naming any inventor.
champagne-cup: Champagne cup is one of the light cups that Victorian and Edwardian hosts mixed by the bowl for dances and garden parties, sparkling wine stretched with a little brandy and liqueur over fruit, and no creator is recorded.
badminton-cup: Jerry Thomas's 1862 bar guide prints it simply as Badminton: half a peeled cucumber steeped with sugar and a little nutmeg in a bottle of claret, then lengthened with a bottle of soda water. The name is usually traced to Badminton House in Gloucestershire, seat of the Dukes of Beaufort, which also gave its name to the game, and no creator of the cup is recorded.
chatham-artillery-punch: An account published in the Augusta Chronicle placed the creation of Chatham Artillery Punch in the 1850s, when the Republican Blues returned to Savannah from a drill in Macon and were welcomed by the Chatham Artillery, a militia unit founded in 1786. A competing legend links it to George Washington's visit to the city, but the original recipe and creator are unknown. It gained national fame after Southern journalists meeting in Savannah in 1870 wrote about it.
mike-collins: The Mike Collins is the Irish whiskey member of the Collins family of tall lemon, sugar and soda drinks, its nickname part of a naming habit that gave each spirit its own Collins, and no creator or date is recorded.
colonel-collins: The Colonel Collins is the bourbon member of the Collins family, its name a nod to the honorary Kentucky colonel that the state's governor still confers, and like the other spirit-named Collinses it has no documented inventor.
applejack-rickey: The Applejack Rickey applies the rickey's rule of lime and soda with no added sugar, a rule born at Shoomaker's bar in Washington, to American apple brandy, and no individual is credited with this version.
gin-buck: Jacques Straub's Drinks of 1914 defines the Gin Buck as a gin rickey made with ginger ale instead of seltzer, and the buck, a spirit topped with ginger ale and sharpened with citrus, was a standard in British and American bars of the early twentieth century. The origin of the name is uncertain, and the mule, made with ginger beer, is a later and more famous relative.
whiskey-buck: The Whiskey Buck is the American whiskey member of the buck family of spirits topped with ginger ale and sharpened with lemon, and no creator or date is recorded for it.
london-buck: The London Buck is the gin buck under the name of the London dry style, which describes a way of making gin rather than a place, and its name is bar shorthand with no recorded creator or date.
mexican-mule: The Mexican Mule swaps tequila into the Moscow Mule, the ginger beer and lime highball that Smirnoff's John G. Martin and Jack Morgan of the Cock 'n' Bull, among others, are credited with launching in America with its copper mug, and no individual is credited with the tequila version.
kentucky-mule: The Kentucky Mule is the bourbon version of the Moscow Mule, the ginger beer and lime highball launched in America to sell Smirnoff vodka in a copper mug, and no individual is credited with putting bourbon in it.
nacional: The Nacional, or Hotel Nacional Special, comes from the Hotel Nacional de Cuba in Havana, which opened at the end of 1930, during American Prohibition. Charles H. Baker's The Gentleman's Companion credited it to Wil P. Taylor, who managed the hotel in the early 1930s, while other accounts name the American bartender Eddie Woelke, and the hotel still serves it.
